questionBank.exp: Asset use efficiency is represented by total asset turnover (Net Sales ÷ Total Assets), distinct from net profit margin (operating efficiency) and the equity multiplier (financial leverage).

questionBank.q: In DuPont analysis, which component captures a company's use of debt to finance its assets, and is also known as the equity multiplier?
questionBank.exp: Financial leverage, measured as the equity multiplier, is an indirect analysis of how much a company relies on debt to finance its assets — the third of the three DuPont drivers alongside net profit margin and asset turnover.

questionBank.q: A company has a net profit margin of 2.4%, an asset turnover of 2.34, and an equity multiplier of 2.94. Using the DuPont breakdown, its return on equity is closest to
questionBank.exp: 2.4% × 2.34 × 2.94 ≈ 16.5%. 5.6% multiplies only margin and turnover (omitting leverage), and 7.6%/22.3% come from other incomplete or reordered combinations of the same three figures.

questionBank.q: Two firms in the same industry report the same return on equity, but DuPont analysis shows one relies heavily on financial leverage while the other relies on a strong net profit margin. What is the main value DuPont analysis adds in this comparison, beyond the plain ROE figure?
opts: It reveals which driver is producing the same ROE
It proves one company's ROE must be miscalculated
It eliminates the need to compute either ROE
It converts ROE into a liquidity measure
questionBank.ans: It reveals which driver is producing the same ROE
questionBank.exp: A DuPont breakdown lets an analyst deduce whether a given ROE is being driven by profitability, asset use, leverage, or a combination — exactly the insight a standalone ROE figure alone cannot provide.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a drawback of DuPont analysis, despite its expanded view of ROE?
opts: It still relies on accounting data that can be manipulated
It cannot be applied to companies with positive net income
It requires audited financial statements to be calculated at all
It only works for companies with no long-term debt
questionBank.ans: It still relies on accounting data that can be manipulated
questionBank.exp: The material lists two drawbacks: DuPont analysis still relies on accounting equations and data that can be manipulated, and it lacks context as to whether the individual ratios should be considered high or low.

questionBank.q: Beyond relying on manipulable accounting data, what other limitation does the material attach to DuPont analysis?
opts: It lacks context on why ratios are high
It cannot be broken into five parts
It requires quarterly, not annual, data
questionBank.ans: It lacks context on why ratios are high
questionBank.exp: Even with its comprehensiveness, DuPont analysis doesn't explain why each component ratio is high or low, or whether it should be considered high or low at all — that judgment still requires additional context.

questionBank.q: A company preparing financial projections to support a bank loan application is primarily seeking to achieve which purpose listed in the material?
questionBank.exp: Raising fresh or additional capital is explicitly listed as a purpose of financial projections, alongside preparing a feasibility study, assuring stakeholders the company has a future, and portraying a financially viable organisation.

questionBank.q: What is described as the ultimate purpose behind preparing financial projections?
opts: To portray a financially viable organisation
To satisfy the external auditor's checklist
To eliminate the need for a cash budget
To replace the statement of cash flows
questionBank.ans: To portray a financially viable organisation
questionBank.exp: The material states the ultimate purpose of financial projections is to portray a financially viable organisation, building on the more specific purposes of raising capital, supporting a feasibility study, and assuring stakeholders.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed under 'what to project' when preparing financial projections?
opts: Forecast of cash available to run the business
The company's historical audit opinion type
questionBank.ans: Forecast of cash available to run the business
questionBank.exp: 'What to project' includes production figures, sales figures, cost and prices of goods/services, forecast of earnings, and forecast of cash available to run the business — not audit opinions, historical share price, or narrative report wording.

questionBank.q: Which of the following questions is explicitly listed under 'how to project' when preparing financial projections?
opts: How well positioned are we to cope with business change?
What was our Chairman's Statement tone last year?
How many shares are currently in issue?
What is our current price earnings ratio?
questionBank.ans: How well positioned are we to cope with business change?
questionBank.exp: 'How to project' includes examining past performance trends, current financial status, how operations were financed historically, how prior problems were overcome, and how well positioned the company is for future change.

questionBank.q: Why does the material say an analyst needs an independent database when working with the assumptions behind a financial projection?
opts: To test the assumptions rather than accept them outright
To satisfy external audit sign-off requirements
To avoid using the company's own sales figures
To calculate the company's DuPont breakdown
questionBank.ans: To test the assumptions rather than accept them outright
questionBank.exp: An independent database is needed to test assumptions — comparing current growth rates against competitors and testing assumptions under different scenarios — not to replace the company's own figures altogether or for audit purposes.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as something to work into the assumptions behind a financial projection?
opts: The wording of the Directors' Report
questionBank.exp: Assumption inputs explicitly listed include the macro/international environment, demand for goods and services, supply of major inputs, banking relationships, production capacity, and labour/community relations.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a factor to review when projecting a company's operating expenses?
questionBank.exp: Operating expense projections should review current market prices, inflation rate, exchange rate, labour pressure, DISCO/energy tariff, petroleum prices, and telecommunication tariffs — not ratios or report opinions, which are separate analytical inputs.

questionBank.q: When deriving a forecast income statement, which step involves expressing the base year's income statement items as percentages of a common figure before projecting forward?
opts: Common sizing the base year Income Statement
questionBank.ans: Common sizing the base year Income Statement
questionBank.exp: Common sizing the base year income statement is one of the explicit steps in deriving a forecast, alongside agreeing the target turnover growth rate, checking the cost structure, determining the effective tax rate, and checking finance charges and the HR budget.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a step in deriving a forecast/abridged income statement?
opts: Determine the effective tax rate to apply
Derive fixed assets from fixed asset turnover
Derive shareholders' funds from the debt ratio
Derive current liabilities from the current ratio
questionBank.ans: Determine the effective tax rate to apply
questionBank.exp: Determining the effective tax rate is a forecast income statement step. The other three options are steps for deriving the forecast statement of financial position instead, not the income statement.

questionBank.q: Which measure provides a single, constant annual growth rate over a multi-year period, calculated as the geometric mean of the period's growth?
questionBank.exp: CAGR is the geometric mean that provides a constant growth rate over several years, calculated as (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1/n) − 1. Trend percentages and horizontal analysis instead compare figures to a base or prior period without smoothing volatility.

questionBank.q: Why does the material favour CAGR over a simple arithmetic mean of yearly growth rates when summarising growth over several years?
opts: CAGR dampens the effect of volatility in periodic growth rates
CAGR requires fewer years of historical data than an arithmetic mean
An arithmetic mean cannot be calculated for negative growth years
CAGR eliminates the need for a base year
questionBank.ans: CAGR dampens the effect of volatility in periodic growth rates
questionBank.exp: CAGR dampens the effects of volatility in periodic growth rates, which can otherwise render a simple arithmetic mean irrelevant or misleading as a summary of overall growth.

questionBank.q: A company's revenue grew from N100 million to N146.4 million over four years. Using the CAGR formula, its compound annual growth rate is closest to
questionBank.exp: CAGR = (146.4/100)^(1/4) − 1 ≈ 10%. 11.6% is a plausible arithmetic-mean-style miscalculation, 46.4% is simply the total percentage growth over the whole period rather than the annualised rate, and 4% wrongly divides the total growth by the number of years.

questionBank.q: When deriving a forecast statement of financial position, shareholders' funds can be derived from the total debt ratio or from which other named ratio?
opts: Current ratio of the base year
questionBank.exp: The material states shareholders' funds can be derived from the total debt ratio or the debt-equity ratio. Current liabilities are instead derived from the base year's current ratio, and fixed assets from the fixed asset turnover ratio.

questionBank.q: When deriving a forecast statement of financial position, from which ratio are a company's forecast current liabilities typically derived?
opts: The current ratio of the base year
questionBank.ans: The current ratio of the base year
questionBank.exp: Current liabilities in a forecast SFP are derived from the base year's current ratio, distinct from total assets (asset turnover), fixed assets (fixed asset turnover), and long-term liabilities/shareholders' funds (debt ratios).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as an input needed to project a company's forecast statement of financial position?
questionBank.exp: Projected SFP inputs explicitly listed include capital expenditure estimates, depreciation policy, stock levels of materials/spares/finished goods, cash positions, and how loan/lease balances are obtained.

questionBank.q: A projection is re-run with a higher assumed exchange rate to observe the effect on revenue and cost, while all other assumptions are held constant. This exercise is best described as
questionBank.exp: Sensitivity analysis involves varying individual assumptions — such as exchange rate, unit price, unit cost, or working hours due to strikes — one at a time to observe the effect on overall projected performance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a factor to vary when performing sensitivity analysis on a financial projection?
opts: Changes in working hours due to strikes or holidays
Changes in the Chairman's Statement tone
Changes in the audit opinion type
Changes in the number of issued shares
questionBank.ans: Changes in working hours due to strikes or holidays
questionBank.exp: Sensitivity analysis factors explicitly listed include unit price and cost changes, exchange/interest/inflation rate changes, and changes in working hours due to strikes, lock-outs, or public holidays.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes a cash budget, according to the material?
opts: A quantitative plan of future action involving strictly the movement of cash
A qualitative narrative of a company's future strategic direction
A restatement of the prior year's audited cash flow statement
A ratio comparing operating cash flow to current liabilities
questionBank.ans: A quantitative plan of future action involving strictly the movement of cash
questionBank.exp: A cash budget is described as a projected statement of future cash flows and a quantitative plan of future action, involving very strictly transactions involving the movement of cash only — not a narrative document or a ratio.

questionBank.q: Over what period can a cash budget be prepared, according to the material?
opts: Almost any period — weekly, monthly, or annually
Only on a strictly annual basis
Only on a strictly monthly basis
Only for periods matching the statutory audit cycle
questionBank.ans: Almost any period — weekly, monthly, or annually
questionBank.exp: The material states cash budgets may be made for almost any period of time, giving weekly, monthly, and annually as examples — there is no fixed statutory period requirement.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a factor that can affect the accuracy of cash budget forecasts?
opts: Inflation, exchange, and interest rate fluctuations
The company's chosen inventory valuation method
The company's number of issued ordinary shares
The wording of the Auditor's Report
questionBank.ans: Inflation, exchange, and interest rate fluctuations
questionBank.exp: The material explicitly notes cash budget forecasts can be affected by adverse or favourable environmental factors such as inflation, exchange rate, and interest rate fluctuations, which is why the underlying assumptions need to be tested for accuracy.

questionBank.q: In a cash budget, how is the closing cash balance for a period arrived at?
opts: The net surplus/deficit is added to the opening balance
The net surplus/deficit is added to total outflow
The opening balance is subtracted from total inflow
The closing balance equals total inflow alone
questionBank.ans: The net surplus/deficit is added to the opening balance
questionBank.exp: The cash budget arrives at a net position (surplus or deficit) from inflows minus outflows, then adds the opening period balance to that net position — the result is the period's closing balance.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a benefit a financial manager gains from preparing a cash budget?
opts: Better ability to plan financing of future cash needs
A reduction in the company's audit fee
An automatic increase in the current ratio
Elimination of the statement of cash flows
questionBank.ans: Better ability to plan financing of future cash needs
questionBank.exp: Cash budget benefits explicitly listed include determining future cash needs, planning for their financing, exercising control over liquidity, and recognising financing and investing activities — not reducing audit fees or replacing the cash flow statement.

questionBank.q: Amaka Textiles Ltd sells 70% of its output on credit; the remaining 30% is cash sales. Of credit sales, 50% is collected in the month following the sale and 50% two months after. If March credit sales are N42,000, how much of that amount is collected in April?
questionBank.exp: 50% of the N42,000 credit sales is collected in the month following the sale: 42,000 × 50% = N21,000. N29,400 mistakenly uses the 70% credit-sales proportion instead of the 50% collection proportion, and N12,600 applies the 30% cash-sales rate instead.

questionBank.q: Using the same company, Amaka Textiles Ltd, total sales for March were N60,000, of which 70% (N42,000) was on credit. What was the value of March's cash sales, collected immediately?
questionBank.exp: Cash sales are the remaining 30% of total sales: 60,000 × 30% = N18,000. N42,000 is the credit sales figure itself, mistaken for the cash portion.

questionBank.q: A company's forecast shows purchases of the following month's anticipated sales are paid for in the preceding month. If April's forecast sales are N60,000 and cost of goods sold is 80% of sales, how much is paid for purchases in March?
questionBank.exp: April's purchases (paid in March, per the one-month-early payment policy) equal 80% of April's forecast sales: 60,000 × 80% = N48,000. N38,400 mistakenly applies 80% twice (of an already-reduced figure), a common compounding error.

questionBank.q: A cash budget line item covers interest paid quarterly on a fixed-rate debenture. If the debenture is N100 million at a 6% annual rate, what is the interest payment due in each quarter it falls due?
questionBank.exp: Annual interest = 100,000,000 × 6% = N6,000,000. Since it's paid quarterly (twice, per a semi-annual debenture schedule as in the worked example) or split across the year, each due payment of N1,500,000 corresponds to a quarter's worth (6,000,000 ÷ 4).

questionBank.q: What is working capital?
opts: The difference between current assets and current liabilities.
The total value of all assets owned by a company.
The amount of cash available for long-term investments.
The total amount of shareholder equity.
questionBank.ans: The difference between current assets and current liabilities.
questionBank.exp: Working capital (or net working capital) is defined as the difference between current assets and current liabilities. It represents the company's ability to meet its short-term obligations. Total assets, cash for long-term investments, and shareholder equity are not working capital.

questionBank.q: Working capital management primarily focuses on:
opts: Managing short-term assets and liabilities to ensure adequate liquidity and efficient operations.
Managing long-term debt and equity financing.
Maximizing the company's share price through dividend policy.
Determining the company's capital expenditure budget.
questionBank.ans: Managing short-term assets and liabilities to ensure adequate liquidity and efficient operations.
questionBank.exp: Working capital management deals with the short-term investment and financing of a company — managing current assets (cash, inventory, receivables) and current liabilities (payables, accruals) to ensure adequate cash flow for operations and productive use of resources. Long-term financing, dividends, and capital expenditure are not the focus.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a goal of working capital management?
opts: Ensuring adequate cash flow for operations.
questionBank.ans: Ensuring adequate cash flow for operations.
questionBank.exp: The goals of working capital management include ensuring adequate cash flow for operations and making the most productive use of resources. Maximizing tax liability, minimizing inventory turnover, and maximizing debt-to-equity are not goals — they would be counterproductive.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a component of working capital?
questionBank.exp: Working capital consists of current assets and current liabilities. Cash, accounts receivable, and accounts payable are all current items. Property, plant, and equipment are non-current (fixed) assets and are not part of working capital.

questionBank.q: Net working capital is calculated as:
opts: Current assets divided by current liabilities.
questionBank.exp: Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. A positive NWC indicates the company can cover its short-term obligations. Total assets minus total liabilities gives net assets (equity); current assets divided by current liabilities gives the current ratio; the inverse is not standard.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a spontaneous source of financing?
questionBank.exp: Trade creditors (accounts payable) are spontaneous financing because they arise automatically from normal business operations (purchases on credit) without formal negotiation. Bank overdrafts, commercial paper, and term loans require active negotiation or formal arrangements.

questionBank.q: Which of the following best describes the working capital cycle?
opts: The time it takes for a company to convert its investments in inventory and other assets into cash through sales.
The time it takes for a company to build a new factory.
The time it takes to collect a company's long-term debt.
The time it takes for a company to prepare its financial statements.
questionBank.ans: The time it takes for a company to convert its investments in inventory and other assets into cash through sales.
questionBank.exp: The working capital cycle (also called the operating cycle or asset conversion cycle) measures the time it takes to convert investments in inventory and other assets into cash through sales. Building a factory, collecting long-term debt, and preparing financial statements are not part of this cycle.

questionBank.q: A company has a positive net working capital. This means:
opts: Its current assets exceed its current liabilities, indicating it can meet short-term obligations.
Its total assets exceed its total liabilities, indicating solvency.
Its current liabilities exceed its current assets, indicating liquidity problems.
questionBank.ans: Its current assets exceed its current liabilities, indicating it can meet short-term obligations.
questionBank.exp: Positive net working capital (current assets > current liabilities) indicates the company has sufficient current assets to cover its short-term obligations. Total assets exceeding total liabilities describes solvency, not working capital; current liabilities exceeding current assets is negative working capital; positive NWC does not mean no debt.

questionBank.q: The operating cycle is calculated as:
opts: Inventory days on hand + Accounts receivable days on hand.
Inventory days on hand − Accounts payable days on hand.
Accounts receivable days + Accounts payable days.
questionBank.ans: Inventory days on hand + Accounts receivable days on hand.
questionBank.exp: The operating cycle = Inventory Days on Hand (InvDOH) + Accounts Receivable Days on Hand (ARDOH). It measures the total time from acquiring inventory to collecting cash from customers. The cash conversion cycle subtracts AP days; the other formulas are incorrect.

questionBank.q: The cash conversion cycle (financing need) is calculated as:
opts: Operating cycle − Accounts payable days on hand.
Inventory days + Receivable days + Payable days.
Operating cycle + Accounts payable days on hand.
Accounts receivable days − Inventory days − Payable days.
questionBank.ans: Operating cycle − Accounts payable days on hand.
questionBank.exp: Cash Conversion Cycle = Operating Cycle − Accounts Payable Days on Hand. It measures the number of days the company needs external financing. Adding AP days or other combinations are incorrect.

questionBank.q: A company has inventory days of 60, accounts receivable days of 30, and accounts payable days of 25. What is its operating cycle?
questionBank.exp: Operating Cycle = InvDOH + ARDOH = 60 + 30 = 90 days. 65 is 60+5; 85 is 60+25; 55 is the cash conversion cycle (60+30−25).

questionBank.q: Using the same data as Q239 (InvDOH=60, ARDOH=30, APDOH=25), what is the cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH = (60 + 30) − 25 = 90 − 25 = 65 days. This is the number of days the company needs external financing. 90 is the operating cycle; 55 is a misapplication; 85 is 60+25.

questionBank.q: A company has an operating cycle of 120 days and a cash conversion cycle of 80 days. What is its accounts payable days on hand?
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH → 80 = 120 − APDOH → APDOH = 40 days. This is the payment period. 200 is 120+80; 80 is the CCC; 120 is the operating cycle.

questionBank.q: A company with a long cash conversion cycle is likely to:
opts: Require more financing to support its operations.
questionBank.ans: Require more financing to support its operations.
questionBank.exp: A longer cash conversion cycle means the company is 'out of cash' for more days — it needs more financing to cover the gap between paying suppliers and collecting from customers. Generating more cash, shorter inventory periods, and faster collection would all shorten the CCC.

questionBank.q: Which of the following actions would reduce a company's cash conversion cycle?
opts: Reducing accounts payable days on hand.
questionBank.exp: CCC = InvDOH + ARDOH − APDOH. Reducing InvDOH or ARDOH, or increasing APDOH, reduces CCC. Slowing collection and increasing InvDOH would increase it; reducing APDOH would also increase it (less credit from suppliers).

questionBank.q: A company has average inventory of ₦400,000, COGS of ₦2,000,000, average accounts receivable of ₦400,000, net credit sales of ₦3,650,000, and average accounts payable of ₦300,000 with purchases of ₦2,190,000. What is its cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: InvDOH = (400,000 / 2,000,000) × 365 = 73 days. ARDOH = (400,000 / 3,650,000) × 365 = 40 days. APDOH = (300,000 / 2,190,000) × 365 = 50 days. CCC = 73 + 40 − 50 = 63 days. 73 is InvDOH alone; 53 is a misapplication; 83 is InvDOH + 10.

questionBank.q: A company's cash conversion cycle increased from 45 days to 60 days. What is the most likely explanation?
opts: The company is taking longer to sell inventory and/or collect receivables relative to its payment period.
The company has reduced its inventory levels.
The company is paying suppliers more quickly.
The company has increased its cash sales.
questionBank.ans: The company is taking longer to sell inventory and/or collect receivables relative to its payment period.
questionBank.exp: An increase in CCC indicates that the company is taking longer to convert its investments into cash — either inventory days have increased, receivables days have increased, or payables days have decreased. Reducing inventory, paying suppliers more quickly (which reduces AP days), and increasing cash sales would all shorten or reduce the CCC.

questionBank.q: Which of the following industries would typically have the shortest cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: Supermarkets have very fast inventory turnover (few days) and mostly cash sales, giving them the shortest CCC. Heavy machinery, real estate, and shipbuilding all have long production cycles and extended collection periods.

questionBank.q: A company has InvDOH of 50 days, ARDOH of 40 days, and APDOH of 35 days. How many days of financing does the company need?
questionBank.exp: Financing Need = CCC = InvDOH + ARDOH − APDOH = 50 + 40 − 35 = 55 days. This is the number of days the company is 'out of cash'. 90 is the operating cycle; 35 is APDOH; 45 is a misapplication.

questionBank.q: A company's financing need is 60 days. If its annual cost of goods sold is ₦3,650,000, what is the approximate amount of working capital financing required?
questionBank.exp: Financing Need Amount = (COGS / 365) × Financing Need in Days = (3,650,000 / 365) × 60 = 10,000 × 60 = ₦600,000. 60,000 would be 6 days; 3,650,000 is total COGS; 10,000 is daily COGS.

questionBank.q: A company has annual COGS of ₦2,190,000 and a cash conversion cycle of 50 days. What is its working capital financing requirement?
questionBank.exp: Daily COGS = 2,190,000 / 365 = ₦6,000. Financing Need = 6,000 × 50 = ₦300,000. 250,000 is for 41.7 days; total COGS is 2,190,000; 100,000 is for 16.7 days.

questionBank.q: If a company reduces its cash conversion cycle from 60 days to 45 days while keeping COGS constant at ₦2,920,000, how much working capital financing is released?
questionBank.exp: Daily COGS = 2,920,000 / 365 = ₦8,000. Reduction in CCC = 15 days. Financing Released = 8,000 × 15 = ₦120,000. 60,000 would be 7.5 days; total COGS is 2,920,000; 180,000 would be 22.5 days.

questionBank.q: The amount of working capital financing required is calculated as:
questionBank.exp: Financing Need Amount = (Annual COGS / 365) × CCC (in days). This converts the days of financing need into a monetary value. Using the operating cycle (which includes AP) would overstate the need; multiplying COGS directly would not account for days; revenue would be incorrect as inventory/purchases drive the need.

questionBank.q: A company has annual COGS of ₦1,825,000 and a cash conversion cycle of 40 days. What is its working capital financing requirement?
questionBank.exp: Daily COGS = 1,825,000 / 365 = ₦5,000. Financing Need = 5,000 × 40 = ₦200,000. 100,000 would be 20 days; total COGS is 1,825,000; 400,000 would be 80 days.

questionBank.q: An aggressive working capital management strategy is characterized by:
opts: Relatively small investment in current assets and relatively large amount of short-term debt.
Relatively large investment in current assets and relatively small amount of short-term debt.
Moderate investment in current assets and moderate short-term debt.
questionBank.ans: Relatively small investment in current assets and relatively large amount of short-term debt.
questionBank.exp: An aggressive strategy minimizes investment in current assets and relies heavily on short-term debt (which is cheaper but riskier). This increases profitability potential but also increases liquidity risk. A large investment in current assets with low debt is conservative; moderate is the moderate strategy.

questionBank.q: A conservative working capital management strategy is characterized by:
opts: Relatively large investment in current assets and relatively small amount of short-term debt.
Relatively small investment in current assets and relatively large amount of short-term debt.
Moderate investment in current assets and moderate short-term debt.
questionBank.ans: Relatively large investment in current assets and relatively small amount of short-term debt.
questionBank.exp: A conservative strategy maintains a large buffer of current assets (e.g., high cash, large inventory) and uses minimal short-term debt, relying more on long-term financing. This reduces liquidity risk but may lower returns. Small current assets with large short-term debt is aggressive; moderate is the middle path.

questionBank.q: A moderate working capital management strategy is characterized by:
opts: Moderate investment in current assets and moderate amount of short-term debt.
Relatively large investment in current assets and relatively small amount of short-term debt.
Relatively small investment in current assets and relatively large amount of short-term debt.
questionBank.ans: Moderate investment in current assets and moderate amount of short-term debt.
questionBank.exp: A moderate strategy takes a balanced approach — neither too much nor too little investment in current assets, and moderate reliance on short-term debt. This aims to balance risk and return. Large investment with low debt is conservative; small investment with high debt is aggressive.

questionBank.q: Which working capital management strategy is most likely to maximize profitability but also carries the highest liquidity risk?
questionBank.exp: The aggressive strategy minimizes investment in current assets and maximizes short-term debt, which can boost returns (less idle cash, lower financing costs) but exposes the company to higher liquidity risk if cash flows are insufficient. Conservative lowers risk but also lowers returns; moderate balances both.

questionBank.q: Which working capital management strategy is most likely to minimize liquidity risk but may reduce profitability?
questionBank.exp: The conservative strategy maintains high current assets (cash, inventory) and uses less short-term debt, reducing the risk of running out of cash. However, idle cash and excess inventory may reduce overall profitability. Aggressive does the opposite; moderate balances both.

questionBank.q: A company that uses short-term debt to finance its entire working investment requirement is following which strategy?
questionBank.exp: Using short-term debt for all working capital needs is the most aggressive approach — it minimizes cost but maximizes refinancing risk. Conservative would use more long-term financing; moderate would balance both; perfect matching would match asset life to financing but would still be less aggressive than using all short-term debt.

questionBank.q: A company that uses long-term financing for its permanent working capital and short-term debt for its seasonal needs is following which strategy?
questionBank.exp: A moderate strategy matches financing to asset types: long-term financing for permanent working capital and fixed assets, short-term debt for seasonal or temporary needs. This balances risk and cost. Aggressive would use short-term for everything; conservative would use long-term for everything.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT an internal factor affecting working capital needs?
questionBank.exp: Interest rates are an external factor (determined by the economy and central bank). Company size, organizational structure, and management sophistication are internal factors that the company can control or influence.

questionBank.q: Overtrading occurs when:
opts: A company expands sales without adequate support from capital, leading to a shortage of liquid funds.
A company has too much investment in current assets and small current liabilities.
A company has very high profitability and low debt.
A company has very low sales volume.
questionBank.ans: A company expands sales without adequate support from capital, leading to a shortage of liquid funds.
questionBank.exp: Overtrading happens when a company tries to expand sales too quickly without sufficient capital (equity or long-term funding), leading to liquidity shortages. It is characterized by low proprietary ratio, low current ratio, and inadequate working capital. Too much investment in current assets is under-trading; high profitability and low debt are not overtrading.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a symptom of overtrading?
opts: The company takes a comparatively long time to pay off its creditors.
The company has a very high current ratio.
The company has lower turnover ratios.
The company has excessive cash balances.
questionBank.ans: The company takes a comparatively long time to pay off its creditors.
questionBank.exp: Overtrading symptoms include taking longer to pay creditors, creditors increasing more rapidly than debtors, declining profits, and excessive borrowing relative to assets owned by shareholders. High current ratio, lower turnover ratios, and excessive cash balances are symptoms of under-trading.

questionBank.q: A company with a low proprietary ratio (equity/assets) and a low current ratio is most likely experiencing:
questionBank.exp: Overtrading is characterized by low proprietary ratio (limited equity capital) and low current ratio (inadequate working capital). The company has expanded beyond its capital base. Under-trading would have high ratios; high profitability and excellent liquidity are not consistent with low ratios.

questionBank.q: Under-trading occurs when:
opts: A company has too much investment in current assets and smaller current liabilities.
A company expands sales without adequate capital support.
A company has insufficient current assets.
questionBank.ans: A company has too much investment in current assets and smaller current liabilities.
questionBank.exp: Under-trading is the opposite of overtrading — it occurs when a company has too much investment in current assets (excess idle cash, high inventory) and too few current liabilities. This often results in lower turnover ratios and reduced profits. Insufficient current assets and over-leverage describe overtrading.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a symptom of under-trading?
opts: A very high current ratio and liquid ratio.
A low current ratio and liquid ratio.
The company takes a long time to pay creditors.
The company has declining profitability due to excessive debt.
questionBank.ans: A very high current ratio and liquid ratio.
questionBank.exp: Under-trading symptoms include very high current and liquid ratios (excess idle funds), lower turnover ratios, reduced profits, loss of goodwill, and falling share prices. Low current ratio, slow creditor payment, and declining profitability due to debt are symptoms of overtrading.

questionBank.q: The consequences of under-trading include all of the following EXCEPT:
opts: Increased liquidity risk due to insufficient current assets.
Reduction in the rate of return on capital employed.
questionBank.ans: Increased liquidity risk due to insufficient current assets.
questionBank.exp: Under-trading involves excessive current assets, so liquidity risk is actually low (too much liquidity). The consequences include reduced profits, lower returns on capital employed, loss of goodwill, and falling share prices. Increased liquidity risk would be a consequence of overtrading.

questionBank.q: A company with a very high current ratio and very low asset turnover is most likely suffering from:
questionBank.exp: Under-trading is characterized by very high current ratios (excess idle funds tied up in current assets) and lower turnover ratios (assets not being used efficiently). Overtrading would have low current ratios; high profitability would not be consistent with low turnover; excessive leverage is not indicated by high current ratio.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a potential cause of overtrading?
opts: Rapid expansion of sales without sufficient equity capital.
High profitability leading to retained earnings.
questionBank.ans: Rapid expansion of sales without sufficient equity capital.
questionBank.exp: Overtrading is caused by expanding sales too quickly without adequate capital support — the company grows faster than its funding base allows. Excessive cash reserves, conservative dividends, and high retained earnings would actually help prevent overtrading by providing more capital.

questionBank.q: A company has annual purchases of ₦1,000,000 and average accounts payable of ₦150,000. What is its accounts payable days on hand?
questionBank.exp: AP Days on Hand = (Average AP / Purchases) × 365 = (150,000 / 1,000,000) × 365 = 0.15 × 365 = 54.8 days. Using 100,000/1,000,000 gives 36.5; using 200,000/1,000,000 gives 73; a misapplication gives 45.6.

questionBank.q: A company has annual COGS of ₦2,000,000 and average inventory of ₦400,000. What is its inventory days on hand?
A company has net credit sales of ₦3,000,000 and average accounts receivable of ₦300,000. What is its accounts receivable days on hand?
A company has an inventory turnover of 8.0. What is its inventory days on hand (approximately)?
questionBank.exp: Inventory Days on Hand = 365 / Inventory Turnover = 365 / 8.0 = 45.6 days. Turnover of 12.2 gives 30 days; turnover of 6.1 gives 60 days; turnover of 24.3 gives 15 days.

questionBank.q: A company has an accounts receivable turnover of 10.0. What is its average collection period?
questionBank.exp: Average Collection Period = 365 / AR Turnover = 365 / 10.0 = 36.5 days. Turnover of 12.2 gives 30 days; turnover of 8.0 gives 45.6 days; turnover of 6.1 gives 60 days.

questionBank.q: A company has an accounts payable turnover of 8.0. What is its accounts payable days on hand?
questionBank.exp: AP Days on Hand = 365 / AP Turnover = 365 / 8.0 = 45.6 days. Turnover of 10.0 gives 36.5 days; turnover of 6.1 gives 60 days; turnover of 12.2 gives 30 days.

questionBank.q: A company's inventory turnover ratio is 6.0 and its accounts receivable turnover is 9.0. If its accounts payable turnover is 5.0, what is its cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: InvDOH = 365 / 6.0 = 60.8 days. ARDOH = 365 / 9.0 = 40.6 days. APDOH = 365 / 5.0 = 73.0 days. CCC = 60.8 + 40.6 − 73.0 = 28.4 days. Adding all gives 174.4; the other operations are incorrect.

questionBank.q: A company's inventory days on hand increased from 40 to 55 days while its COGS remained constant. The most likely explanation is:
opts: The company is carrying more inventory relative to sales.
The company is selling inventory more quickly.
The company's suppliers have extended their credit terms.
The company's gross profit margin has increased.
questionBank.ans: The company is carrying more inventory relative to sales.
questionBank.exp: Inventory Days = (Average Inventory / COGS) × 365. If COGS is constant, an increase in days means higher average inventory — the company is holding more stock. Selling more quickly would reduce days; extended supplier credit affects AP days, not inventory; gross margin is unrelated.

questionBank.q: A company's accounts receivable days on hand increased from 35 to 50 days. What is the most likely concern?
opts: The company is taking longer to collect cash from customers, potentially increasing credit risk.
The company is collecting cash from customers more quickly.
The company has improved its credit policy.
The company's sales have decreased significantly.
questionBank.ans: The company is taking longer to collect cash from customers, potentially increasing credit risk.
questionBank.exp: An increase in AR days means customers are taking longer to pay, which can indicate loosening credit terms or collection problems. This may increase the risk of bad debts. Faster collection would decrease days; improved credit policy would also decrease days; decreased sales could affect the ratio but the primary concern is slower collection.

questionBank.q: A company's accounts payable days on hand decreased from 50 to 35 days. This likely means:
opts: The company is paying its suppliers more quickly.
The company is taking longer to pay its suppliers.
The company has increased its inventory purchases.
questionBank.ans: The company is paying its suppliers more quickly.
questionBank.exp: AP days measure how long the company takes to pay suppliers. A decrease from 50 to 35 means the company is paying faster — which may reduce its cash conversion cycle (less credit) but could strain cash flow. Taking longer would increase days; increased purchases would not necessarily change the ratio unless the average AP changes differently.

questionBank.q: A company's cash conversion cycle is 45 days. If the company wants to reduce it to 30 days, which of the following actions would achieve this?
opts: Increasing accounts receivable days by 15 days.
Reducing accounts payable days by 15 days.
Increasing the operating cycle by 15 days.
questionBank.exp: CCC = InvDOH + ARDOH − APDOH. Reducing InvDOH by 15 days reduces CCC by 15 days. Increasing AR days would increase CCC; reducing AP days would increase CCC (less supplier credit); increasing the operating cycle would also increase CCC.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would NOT be a symptom of overtrading?
opts: Very high current ratio and liquidity ratio.
Low current ratio and liquidity ratio.
Creditors increasing more rapidly than debtors.
questionBank.ans: Very high current ratio and liquidity ratio.
questionBank.exp: Overtrading symptoms include low current and liquidity ratios, creditors rising faster than debtors, low proprietary ratio, declining profits, and excessive borrowing. Very high current and liquidity ratios are symptoms of under-trading, not overtrading.

questionBank.q: A company with a very low cash conversion cycle is likely to:
opts: Require less external financing for its operations.
questionBank.ans: Require less external financing for its operations.
questionBank.exp: A low cash conversion cycle means the company converts its investments into cash quickly, so it needs less external financing. High inventory and long collection periods would increase the CCC, not decrease it.

questionBank.q: A company has decided to offer extended credit terms to customers to boost sales. What is the likely impact on its cash conversion cycle?
opts: It will increase because accounts receivable days will increase.
It will decrease because sales will increase.
It will remain unchanged because inventory and payables are unaffected.
It will increase because accounts payable days will increase.
questionBank.ans: It will increase because accounts receivable days will increase.
questionBank.exp: Extended credit terms increase the time customers take to pay → ARDOH increases → CCC increases (longer financing need). While sales may increase, the immediate effect on the CCC is an increase in AR days. AP days are not affected by this decision.

questionBank.q: A company has negotiated longer payment terms with its suppliers. What is the likely impact on its cash conversion cycle?
opts: It will decrease because accounts payable days will increase.
It will increase because accounts payable days will increase.
It will remain unchanged because inventory and receivables are unaffected.
It will increase because inventory days will increase.
questionBank.ans: It will decrease because accounts payable days will increase.
questionBank.exp: Extended supplier credit increases APDOH → CCC decreases (shorter financing need) because the company can delay cash outflows. While inventory and receivables are unaffected, the CCC will decrease, not increase.

questionBank.q: A company has an operating cycle of 100 days and pays its suppliers in 40 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH = 100 − 40 = 60 days. This is the financing need. 140 would be adding instead of subtracting; 100 is the operating cycle; 40 is APDOH.

questionBank.q: A company's cash conversion cycle is 30 days. If its operating cycle is 90 days, what is its accounts payable days on hand?
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH → 30 = 90 − APDOH → APDOH = 60 days. 30 is CCC; 90 is operating cycle; 120 is 90+30.

questionBank.q: In the context of working capital management, spontaneous financing refers to:
opts: Financing that arises automatically from business operations, such as trade credit.
Financing obtained through negotiation with banks.
Financing obtained through the issuance of shares.
Financing with a fixed maturity date.
questionBank.ans: Financing that arises automatically from business operations, such as trade credit.
questionBank.exp: Spontaneous financing arises from normal business operations without formal negotiation — primarily trade creditors (accounts payable) and accruals. Bank loans, share issuance, and fixed-maturity financing are not spontaneous because they require active arrangement.

questionBank.q: A company's current ratio is 2.5 and its quick ratio is 1.2. This suggests that:
opts: Inventory represents a significant portion of current assets.
The company has very little inventory.
The company has excessive cash balances.
The company has no accounts receivable.
questionBank.ans: Inventory represents a significant portion of current assets.
questionBank.exp: The difference between current ratio (which includes inventory) and quick ratio (which excludes it) is explained by inventory. A gap of 1.3 (2.5 − 1.2) indicates inventory is a material part of current assets. Little inventory would make the ratios closer; excessive cash would make both ratios high; no AR would lower the quick ratio relative to current.

questionBank.q: A company has current assets of ₦800,000, current liabilities of ₦400,000, and inventory of ₦200,000. What is its net working capital and quick ratio respectively?
A company's annual sales are ₦5,000,000, all on credit. Its average collection period is 45 days. What is its average accounts receivable?
A company's annual COGS is ₦3,000,000 and its inventory turnover is 6.0. What is its average inventory?
questionBank.exp: Average Inventory = COGS / Inventory Turnover = 3,000,000 / 6.0 = ₦500,000. 600,000 would be turnover of 5.0; 18,000,000 is COGS × 6; 3,000,000 is COGS.

questionBank.q: A company's annual purchases are ₦2,400,000 and its accounts payable turnover is 8.0. What is its average accounts payable?
questionBank.exp: Average AP = Purchases / AP Turnover = 2,400,000 / 8.0 = ₦300,000. 400,000 would be turnover of 6.0; 19,200,000 is purchases × 8; 2,400,000 is purchases.

questionBank.q: A company has average inventory of ₦250,000, annual COGS of ₦1,500,000, average AR of ₦200,000, annual credit sales of ₦2,400,000, average AP of ₦180,000, and annual purchases of ₦1,500,000. What is its cash conversion cycle in days?
questionBank.exp: InvDOH = (250,000 / 1,500,000) × 365 = 60.8 days. ARDOH = (200,000 / 2,400,000) × 365 = 30.4 days. APDOH = (180,000 / 1,500,000) × 365 = 43.8 days. CCC = 60.8 + 30.4 − 43.8 = 47.4 days. Adding all gives 135 days; the other operations are incorrect.

questionBank.q: A company with a cash conversion cycle of 50 days and annual COGS of ₦3,650,000 has a working capital financing requirement of:
questionBank.exp: Daily COGS = 3,650,000 / 365 = ₦10,000. Financing Need = 10,000 × 50 = ₦500,000. 100,000 is for 10 days; total COGS is 3,650,000; 1,000,000 is for 100 days.

questionBank.q: If a company's operating cycle is 80 days and its cash conversion cycle is 45 days, the company's average payment period to suppliers is:
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH → 45 = 80 − APDOH → APDOH = 35 days. This is the payment period. 45 is CCC; 80 is operating cycle; 125 is 80+45.

questionBank.q: A company's inventory turnover ratio has decreased from 8.0 to 6.0. The most likely implication is:
opts: The company is selling its inventory more slowly, which may increase holding costs and reduce cash flow.
The company is selling its inventory more quickly.
The company's gross profit margin has increased.
The company's suppliers have reduced their prices.
questionBank.ans: The company is selling its inventory more slowly, which may increase holding costs and reduce cash flow.
questionBank.exp: A lower inventory turnover means inventory is being sold more slowly — goods are sitting longer. This increases holding costs, the risk of obsolescence, and ties up cash. Selling more quickly would increase turnover; gross margin and supplier prices do not directly determine turnover.

questionBank.q: A company's accounts receivable turnover ratio has increased from 6.0 to 9.0. This indicates:
opts: The company is collecting its receivables more quickly.
The company is collecting receivables more slowly.
The company has extended credit terms.
questionBank.ans: The company is collecting its receivables more quickly.
questionBank.exp: An increase in AR turnover means the company is collecting its receivables more times per year — i.e., more quickly. Slower collection and extended credit terms would decrease turnover; decreased sales could affect the ratio but the primary interpretation is faster collection.

questionBank.q: A company's accounts payable turnover ratio has decreased from 10.0 to 7.0. This likely means:
opts: The company is taking longer to pay its suppliers.
The company is paying its suppliers more quickly.
The company has increased its purchases.
The company has reduced its credit terms.
questionBank.ans: The company is taking longer to pay its suppliers.
questionBank.exp: A lower AP turnover means fewer payment cycles per year — the company is taking longer to pay its suppliers. More quickly would increase turnover; increased purchases alone would not necessarily decrease turnover; reduced credit terms would likely increase turnover.

questionBank.q: A company has an operating cycle of 75 days and pays suppliers in 30 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: CCC = 75 − 30 = 45 days. 105 would be adding; 75 is the operating cycle; 30 is APDOH.

questionBank.q: A company has a cash conversion cycle of 35 days and pays suppliers in 40 days. What is its operating cycle?
questionBank.exp: CCC = Operating Cycle − APDOH → 35 = Operating Cycle − 40 → Operating Cycle = 75 days. 5 would be 40-35; 35 is CCC; 40 is APDOH.

questionBank.q: Which of the following would most likely indicate that a company is overtrading?
opts: A low current ratio combined with rapid sales growth and limited equity capital.
A high current ratio combined with high inventory turnover.
A low debt-to-equity ratio and high profit margin.
A high cash conversion cycle and low inventory levels.
questionBank.ans: A low current ratio combined with rapid sales growth and limited equity capital.
questionBank.exp: Overtrading is characterized by low current ratio (liquidity strain), rapid sales growth, and limited equity capital (low proprietary ratio). High current ratio, low debt, high profit, and high cash conversion with low inventory are not consistent with overtrading.

questionBank.q: A company has current assets of ₦600,000, current liabilities of ₦250,000, and inventory of ₦150,000. Its current ratio and quick ratio respectively are:
questionBank.exp: Current Ratio = 600,000 / 250,000 = 2.4. Quick Ratio = (600,000 − 150,000) / 250,000 = 450,000 / 250,000 = 1.8. 2.4 and 1.2 would use a different inventory figure; the other options have the ratios swapped.

questionBank.q: A company has working capital of ₦300,000 and current liabilities of ₦200,000. What are its current assets and current ratio respectively?
questionBank.exp: NWC = CA − CL → 300,000 = CA − 200,000 → CA = ₦500,000. Current Ratio = 500,000 / 200,000 = 2.5. 300,000 would be CA if CL were 0; 2.0 would be 400,000/200,000; 1.0 would be equal.

questionBank.q: A company has annual sales of ₦10,000,000, all on credit, and an average collection period of 60 days. What is its average accounts receivable?
Every business goes through a cycle made up of two main elements: the asset conversion (operating) cycle and which other cycle?
questionBank.exp: The business cycle consists of the asset conversion (operating) cycle — turning resources into cash through sales — and the capital investment cycle, which covers acquisition, use, and disposal of long-term assets.

questionBank.q: The material states that understanding both the asset conversion cycle and the capital investment cycle is essential for effective business management because of their impact on which three things?
opts: Cash flow, profitability, and overall performance
Working capital, gearing, and dividend policy
questionBank.ans: Cash flow, profitability, and overall performance
questionBank.exp: The material explicitly states these two cycles impact a company's cash flow, profitability, and overall performance — which is why understanding both is described as essential to effective business management.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is one of the four stages explicitly listed in the asset conversion (operating) cycle?
questionBank.exp: The operating cycle's four stages are procurement of inputs, manufacturing and production, sales, and collection — not capital budgeting, loan disbursement, or dividend declaration, which belong to other financial processes.

questionBank.q: Which formula correctly calculates the operating cycle?
opts: Inventory Holding Period + Receivables Collection Period
Inventory Holding Period − Receivables Collection Period
questionBank.ans: Inventory Holding Period + Receivables Collection Period
questionBank.exp: The operating cycle is Inventory Holding Period + Receivables Collection Period. The net operating (cash conversion) cycle then subtracts the payment period from this figure.

questionBank.q: A company holds inventory for 44 days and collects receivables in 41 days, and pays its suppliers after 26 days. What is its cash conversion cycle?
questionBank.exp: Operating cycle = 44 + 41 = 85 days. Cash conversion cycle = 85 − 26 = 59 days. 85 days is the operating cycle mistaken for the cash conversion cycle, and 111 days wrongly adds the payment period instead of subtracting it.

questionBank.q: A borrower has InvDOH of 45 days and ARDOH of 35 days, and pays creditors after 37 days. How many days of financing does the company need to cover its operating cycle?
questionBank.exp: Operating cycle = 45 + 35 = 80 days. Financing need = 80 − 37 = 43 days. 80 days is the operating cycle itself, mistaken for the financing need before subtracting the payment period.

questionBank.q: In the example where a borrower needs financing for 43 out of an 80-day operating cycle, from which sources does the material say this financing may come?
opts: Internal profits, or outside sources like bank financing
Only from the sale of long-term fixed assets
Only from issuing new ordinary shares
questionBank.ans: Internal profits, or outside sources like bank financing
questionBank.exp: The material notes this financing need may be provided from internal cash sources such as available profits, or from outside sources such as bank financing — not restricted to asset sales, new equity, or delaying statutory payments.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly defines 'trading assets' as used in estimating working investment?
questionBank.exp: Trading assets are defined as all of a company's current assets excluding cash — specifically accounts receivable plus inventory — used as a quick way to estimate financing needs for trading operations.

questionBank.q: Within a company's trading assets, which portion should be financed with long-term sources, according to the material?
questionBank.exp: The material states the seasonal portion of trading assets should be financed short-term, while the core (permanent) portion should be financed long-term — and that long-term financing of the core portion is called working capital.

questionBank.q: Which of the following defines 'spontaneous financing' as used in estimating working investment requirement?
opts: Non-interest-bearing liabilities like trade creditors and expenses payable
All of the company's short-term bank borrowings
The company's long-term debt and equity combined
The company's current assets excluding cash
questionBank.ans: Non-interest-bearing liabilities like trade creditors and expenses payable
questionBank.exp: Spontaneous financing includes all non-interest-bearing liabilities — trade creditors and expenses payable — funds that arise naturally in the course of business without an explicit financing cost.

questionBank.q: A company's trading assets are lower than its spontaneous financing for the period. What does this indicate about its working investment position?
questionBank.exp: When Trading Assets < Spontaneous Financing, the company has a working investment surplus. When Trading Assets > Spontaneous Financing, there is instead a working investment requirement; when the two are equal, no working capital funding is needed.

questionBank.q: Which of the following correctly describes 'working capital available' as distinct from working investment requirement?
opts: The difference between long-term funds and long-term assets
The difference between trading assets and spontaneous financing
The sum of accounts receivable and inventory
The difference between current assets and liabilities
questionBank.ans: The difference between long-term funds and long-term assets
questionBank.exp: Working capital available is the difference between a company's long-term funds (equity and long-term debt) and its long-term assets (fixed and intangible assets) — a distinct concept from the working investment requirement calculated from trading assets.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as an effect of inadequate working capital?
opts: Loss of goodwill and creditworthiness among creditors
An automatic increase in the equity multiplier
A guaranteed improvement in the debt-to-equity ratio
A reduction in the company's fixed asset base
questionBank.ans: Loss of goodwill and creditworthiness among creditors
questionBank.exp: Effects of inadequate working capital explicitly listed include loss of goodwill and creditworthiness, missed favourable opportunities, operational inefficiencies, weakened shock-absorbing capacity, and non-achievement of profit targets.

questionBank.q: Why does inadequate working capital weaken a company's ability to handle unexpected business shocks, according to the material?
opts: It cannot meet contingencies arising from business oscillations or financial losses
It automatically triggers a covenant breach with all lenders
It forces an immediate write-down of fixed assets
It prevents the company from calculating its current ratio
questionBank.ans: It cannot meet contingencies arising from business oscillations or financial losses
questionBank.exp: The material states inadequate working capital weakens the shock-absorbing capacity of the company because it cannot meet contingencies arising from business oscillations or financial losses — a direct, explicitly stated consequence.

questionBank.q: Fatima Toys borrows to fund new equipment so it can double sales, expecting profit to rise from N500,000 to N1 million per cycle. What does the material say about how many production cycles the loan is likely to take to repay?
opts: The loan cannot be repaid from operations
questionBank.exp: Since the loan cannot be repaid in one production cycle at the projected profit level, the material notes Fatima Toys could repay it over three or four production cycles if profitable operations generate enough cash.

questionBank.q: Unlike stock, which is converted to cash through sale, how is a loan used to acquire fixed assets typically expected to be repaid?
opts: In piecemeal instalments from the profit the asset generates
By selling the fixed asset once it has appreciated
In a lump sum from the next operating cycle
Through a write-off against retained earnings
questionBank.ans: In piecemeal instalments from the profit the asset generates
questionBank.exp: A loan for fixed assets is not repaid by selling the asset itself — repayment instead comes in piecemeal as profit is made from using the asset, which increases cash flow available for repayment.

questionBank.q: How does the material define net working capital?
opts: Total current assets less total current liabilities
questionBank.ans: Total current assets less total current liabilities
questionBank.exp: Net working capital is defined as total current assets less total current liabilities — a distinct figure from trading assets less spontaneous financing (working investment) or long-term funds less long-term assets (working capital available).

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an internal factor affecting a company's working capital needs, rather than an external one?
questionBank.exp: Internal factors listed include company size and growth rate, organisational structure, sophistication of working capital management, and borrowing/investing capacity. Interest rates, the economy, and competitors are all listed as external factors.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is listed as an external factor affecting a company's working capital needs, rather than an internal one?
questionBank.exp: External factors listed include banking services, interest rates, new technologies and products, the economy, and competitors — as opposed to internal factors such as company size, structure, and management sophistication.

questionBank.q: Which working capital period represents the time it takes a company to convert raw materials into finished goods?
questionBank.exp: The manufacturing period covers converting raw materials into finished goods — the longer this period, the more cash is tied up in production. The inventory period instead covers how long finished goods sit before sale.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a key activity within the manufacturing period?
questionBank.exp: The manufacturing period's key activities are sourcing and procurement, production and processing, quality control and inspection, and storage of work-in-progress. Aging of receivables and payment discounts belong to the collection and payment periods respectively.

questionBank.q: Which working capital period measures how long it takes a company to sell its finished goods, and has an inverse relationship with the inventory turnover ratio?
questionBank.exp: The inventory period measures time to sell finished goods and is inversely related to inventory turnover — a higher turnover corresponds to a shorter inventory period, and vice versa.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a consideration within the inventory period, alongside carrying costs and opportunity costs?
questionBank.exp: The inventory period's key considerations are carrying costs, opportunity costs, and obsolescence/spoilage — inventory that isn't sold quickly can spoil or become obsolete, tying up cash unproductively.

questionBank.q: Which working capital period provides 'spontaneous financing' — interest-free funds that arise naturally in the course of doing business?
questionBank.exp: The payment period — the time a company takes to pay its suppliers — provides spontaneous financing, since the resulting current liabilities are non-interest-bearing while payment is outstanding.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a consideration within the payment period?
questionBank.exp: The payment period's considerations include credit terms, cash flow management, and evaluating early payment discounts — while making sure the supplier relationship is not jeopardised by stretching payment too far.

questionBank.q: Which working capital period has an inverse relationship with the accounts receivable turnover ratio?
questionBank.exp: The collection period — the delay between a sale and cash collection — is inversely related to receivable turnover: a higher turnover means a shorter collection period, and vice versa.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a key consideration within the collection period?
opts: Sourcing and procurement of raw materials
questionBank.exp: The collection period's considerations include credit policies, credit monitoring, and aging of receivables — keeping a close watch on overdue payments so appropriate collection strategies can be deployed.

questionBank.q: A company holds a relatively small investment in current assets alongside a relatively large amount of short-term debt. Which working capital strategy does this describe?
questionBank.exp: The aggressive strategy combines a relatively small investment in current assets with a relatively large amount of short-term debt — the opposite combination to the conservative strategy.

questionBank.q: A company holds a relatively large investment in current assets alongside a relatively small amount of short-term debt. Which working capital strategy does this describe?
questionBank.exp: The conservative strategy combines a relatively large investment in current assets with a relatively small amount of short-term debt — favouring liquidity and lower short-term financing risk over the aggressive strategy's leaner approach.

questionBank.q: Which working capital strategy involves moderate investment in current assets paired with a moderate amount of short-term debt?
questionBank.exp: The moderate strategy sits between the aggressive and conservative approaches, pairing moderate current-asset investment with a moderate level of short-term debt.

questionBank.q: Which condition arises when a company expands its sales volume without adequate supporting capital, leaving it with limited resources relative to its business volume?
questionBank.exp: Overtrading arises when capital employed is inadequate relative to the volume of business — an expansion of sales without adequate capital support, leaving the company suffering from acute shortage of liquid funds.

questionBank.q: What combination of ratios does overtrading typically result in, according to the material?
opts: A low proprietary ratio, low current ratio, and low liquid ratio
A high proprietary ratio, high current ratio, and high liquid ratio
A high current ratio but a low proprietary ratio only
No effect on any liquidity or proprietary ratio
questionBank.ans: A low proprietary ratio, low current ratio, and low liquid ratio
questionBank.exp: Overtrading results in a low proprietary ratio, low current ratio, and low liquid ratio, reflecting inadequate working capital relative to the volume of business — the mirror image of under-trading's high-ratio symptoms.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a symptom of overtrading?
opts: The company increases borrowing excessively relative to shareholders' assets
The company holds an unusually high current ratio
The company reduces its rate of short-term borrowing
Creditor days fall while debtor days rise
questionBank.ans: The company increases borrowing excessively relative to shareholders' assets
questionBank.exp: Listed overtrading symptoms include creditors increasing relative to debtors (or rising more rapidly / falling more slowly), declining profit, excessive borrowing relative to shareholders' assets, buying fixed assets from short-term funds, and unusual bills payable patterns.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a symptom of overtrading involving how a company funds its fixed assets?
opts: Buying fixed or non-current assets out of short-term funds
Buying fixed assets exclusively from retained earnings
Refusing to acquire any new fixed assets
Selling fixed assets to repay short-term creditors
questionBank.ans: Buying fixed or non-current assets out of short-term funds
questionBank.exp: A specifically listed overtrading symptom is a company buying fixed or non-current assets out of short-term funds — mismatching the long-term nature of the asset with short-term financing, a classic overtrading red flag.

questionBank.q: Which condition is described as the opposite of overtrading, arising from too much investment in current assets alongside a smaller amount of current liabilities?
questionBank.exp: Under-trading is the condition contrary to overtrading — an application of idle funds resulting from too much investment in current assets and a smaller amount of current liabilities.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a symptom of under-trading?
opts: A very high current ratio and liquid ratio
A very low current ratio and liquid ratio
Higher turnover ratios than industry peers
A rapid increase in short-term borrowing
questionBank.ans: A very high current ratio and liquid ratio
questionBank.exp: Under-trading's listed symptoms are a very high current ratio and liquid ratio, alongside lower turnover ratios — the mirror image of overtrading's low-ratio symptoms.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a consequence of under-trading?
opts: Fall in the market price of company shares
A sharp rise in short-term borrowing
An increase in the proprietary ratio
questionBank.ans: Fall in the market price of company shares
questionBank.exp: Under-trading's listed consequences are reduced profits, reduced rate of return on capital employed, loss of goodwill, and a fall in the market price of the company's shares.

questionBank.q: Window dressing in financial statements refers to:
opts: Manipulating key financial figures to present a picture that may not accurately reflect the true financial health of the company.
Standardizing financial statements to comply with IFRS.
Adding visual improvements to the annual report design.
Presenting financial data in a more user-friendly format.
questionBank.ans: Manipulating key financial figures to present a picture that may not accurately reflect the true financial health of the company.
questionBank.exp: Window dressing involves manipulating financial figures (e.g., revenue recognition, expense deferral, asset inflation) to present an overly favorable picture. It is a form of creative accounting or fraud, not standardization, design improvements, or user-friendly formatting.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a common technique used in window dressing?
opts: Deliberate understatement of expenses to inflate net income.
Increasing investment in research and development.
Issuing additional shares to raise capital.
questionBank.ans: Deliberate understatement of expenses to inflate net income.
questionBank.exp: Understating expenses is a common window-dressing technique — it artificially inflates net income. Increasing R&D, issuing shares, and paying dividends are legitimate transactions, not typically associated with window dressing.

questionBank.q: A company that defers necessary expenses to future periods is engaging in:
opts: Window dressing by inflating current-period profits.
Window dressing by reducing current-period profits.
questionBank.ans: Window dressing by inflating current-period profits.
questionBank.exp: Deferring necessary expenses to a later period artificially boosts current-period profits by reducing current expenses. This is a form of window dressing (manipulation). It is not legitimate under IFRS if it violates the matching principle and is not conservative accounting.

questionBank.q: Inflating the value of assets on the Statement of Financial Position is a window-dressing technique that primarily affects:
opts: The company's reported financial position and leverage ratios.
The company's cash flow statement only.
questionBank.ans: The company's reported financial position and leverage ratios.
questionBank.exp: Inflating asset values overstates the balance sheet (financial position) and improves leverage ratios (e.g., lower debt ratio). It does not directly affect the cash flow statement or income statement unless depreciation changes, and dividend policy is not directly affected.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is an example of liability understatement as a window-dressing technique?
opts: Deliberately understating unpaid expenses or accrued liabilities.
Increasing accounts payable by recording more purchases.
questionBank.ans: Deliberately understating unpaid expenses or accrued liabilities.
questionBank.exp: Understating liabilities (e.g., unpaid expenses, accruals) reduces reported liabilities and improves leverage ratios. Increasing AP would overstate liabilities; issuing bonds and repaying debt are legitimate transactions, not window dressing.

questionBank.q: A company that manipulates its provisions and reserves to smooth earnings is engaging in:
opts: Earnings management or income smoothing, a form of window dressing.
questionBank.ans: Earnings management or income smoothing, a form of window dressing.
questionBank.exp: Manipulating provisions and reserves to create consistent, stable performance (income smoothing) is a form of earnings management and window dressing. Legitimate accrual accounting applies provisions based on estimates, not for smoothing; cash flow and tax are not the primary focus.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a sign that a company may be engaging in window dressing?
opts: Unusual or unexpected transactions around the end of the reporting period.
Consistent and stable performance with no volatility.
High cash balances and low debt.
questionBank.ans: Unusual or unexpected transactions around the end of the reporting period.
questionBank.exp: Unusual transactions near period-end (e.g., large sales just before year-end, asset sales, debt restructuring) are a red flag for window dressing. Consistent performance could be legitimate but also suspicious; high cash and low debt are not necessarily signs; regular dividends are normal.

questionBank.q: What is a key prevention measure against window dressing?
opts: Implementing strong internal controls and conducting regular independent audits.
Allowing management to choose any accounting policy they prefer.
questionBank.ans: Implementing strong internal controls and conducting regular independent audits.
questionBank.exp: Strong internal controls and independent audits (both internal and external) help detect and prevent manipulation. Allowing free choice of accounting policies, reducing auditors, and eliminating disclosures would increase the risk of window dressing.

questionBank.q: A company that alters the useful life or changes the depreciation method of its assets is potentially engaging in:
opts: Window dressing by changing assumptions to influence reported profits.
Both A and B — it is window dressing if done to manipulate; legitimate if justified and disclosed.
questionBank.ans: Both A and B — it is window dressing if done to manipulate; legitimate if justified and disclosed.
questionBank.exp: Changing useful life or depreciation method can be legitimate if justified by changes in asset usage or economic conditions, properly disclosed, and in line with accounting standards. However, if done solely to manipulate profits, it is window dressing. The correct answer is that it depends on intent and disclosure.

questionBank.q: Creative revenue recognition is a form of window dressing that may involve:
opts: Recording revenue before it is earned or when significant uncertainties remain.
Recording revenue only after cash is received.
Reducing sales prices to increase volume.
questionBank.ans: Recording revenue before it is earned or when significant uncertainties remain.
questionBank.exp: Creative revenue recognition includes recording revenue prematurely (before performance obligations are met, when collectibility is uncertain, or before delivery). Recording only on cash receipt is too conservative; deferring revenue is conservative; reducing sales prices is not revenue recognition manipulation.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a method to guard against window dressing?
opts: Conducting regular reconciliations of financial data.
Reducing the frequency of financial reporting.
questionBank.ans: Conducting regular reconciliations of financial data.
questionBank.exp: Regular reconciliations help detect discrepancies and manipulation. Accepting management's representations without question, reducing reporting frequency, and eliminating internal audit all increase the risk of undetected window dressing.

questionBank.q: A company that enters into off-balance-sheet transactions to hide debt is engaging in:
opts: Window dressing by concealing liabilities from the balance sheet.
questionBank.ans: Window dressing by concealing liabilities from the balance sheet.
questionBank.exp: Off-balance-sheet transactions (e.g., operating leases, special purpose entities) can be used to hide debt and improve leverage ratios — a form of window dressing. While some are legitimate, when used to conceal debt, they are manipulative.

questionBank.q: A company that capitalizes costs that should be expensed immediately is engaging in:
opts: Window dressing by inflating assets and deferring expenses.
questionBank.ans: Window dressing by inflating assets and deferring expenses.
questionBank.exp: Capitalizing costs (e.g., treating repairs as additions to fixed assets) inflates assets and defers expenses to future periods, boosting current profit. This is a form of window dressing. It is not conservative or legitimate if it violates the matching principle.

questionBank.q: Which of the following is the most effective way to detect window dressing?
opts: Analyzing key financial ratios and metrics over time for unusual patterns.
Accepting the auditor's opinion without review.
Looking only at the net income figure.
Ignoring the notes to the financial statements.
questionBank.ans: Analyzing key financial ratios and metrics over time for unusual patterns.
questionBank.exp: Analyzing financial ratios and metrics over time (e.g., sudden changes in gross margin, receivable days, asset turnover) can reveal patterns consistent with manipulation. Accepting opinions without review, looking only at net income, and ignoring notes are all ineffective.

questionBank.q: A company that engages in transactions that are not fully disclosed on the balance sheet is likely:
opts: Attempting to window-dress by hiding assets or liabilities.
questionBank.ans: Attempting to window-dress by hiding assets or liabilities.
